strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a practical limitation of knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift with clear problem formulation and compelling examples

Novel methodological approach combining teacher-student disagreement with guided diffusion to target spurious features, with intuitive design (maximizing teacher confidence while minimizing student confidence)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet) with multiple metrics and extensive ablations demonstrating consistent improvements, particularly on worst-group accuracy (66.1% vs 54.0% for ActGen)

Insightful empirical analysis showing ConfiG generates the most challenging samples for students while preserving teacher correctness; qualitative visualizations clearly demonstrate selective modification of spurious vs. causal features
Theoretical justification through Proposition 1 providing formal analysis that ConfiG reduces generalization error under reasonable assumptions, supported by detailed lemmas
Strong reproducibility support with extensive hyperparameter details, multiple ablations on architecture/dataset size, and clear experimental protocols
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: method requires a robust teacher model that generalizes well to both train and test distributions; for SpuCo Birds, authors had to fine-tune ViT-B on balanced data rather than using CLIP (40.2% worst-group accuracy), undermining applicability when robust teachers are unavailable

Substantial computational overhead: 11.4 sec/image (5 optimization steps) vs. 3.3 sec for ActGen—3.5× more expensive; while Table 8 demonstrates quality over quantity, the cost remains significant for practitioners

Limited theoretical depth: Proposition 1 assumes strong conditions (δt + δs < 1/L, teacher accurate globally on Ptest ∪ Ptrain ∪ supp(Q)) and only shows error reduction to min{Ω - Θ, Ω/2} without characterizing improvement magnitude; theorem applies to any augmentations satisfying Eq. 13, not specific to ConfiG's objective

Artificial experimental scope: CelebA and SpuCo Birds use synthetic spurious correlations with deliberately removed groups; real-world biases are subtler; weaker results on Spurious ImageNet (second-best validation accuracy, only 0.5% mAUC improvement over ActGen)

Under-explored design choices: γ=2 selected empirically without ablation; number of optimization steps (5) appears arbitrary; auxiliary student training complexity and sensitivity not analyzed; prompt choice unjustified

Incomplete method comparisons: missing comparisons to group robustness methods without group labels (JUST, JTT); limited to four diffusion-based baselines; no comparison to simple data balancing strategies

Assumptions not fully validated in practice: assumes p*(y|x) invariant under covariate shift (often violated); assumes teacher trained on balanced/representative data (often infeasible); condition on Θ in Proposition 1 complex and difficult to verify a priori

Presentation issues: Figure 1 duplicated (pages 1-2); theoretical contribution relegated to appendix creating narrative disconnect; standard deviations reported but no statistical significance tests; some Spurious ImageNet improvements potentially not statistically significant (93.3% vs 93.0-93.2%)

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: The paper articulates a genuine practical challenge in knowledge distillation under covariate shift with unknown spurious features, with intuitive visual examples

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet), four recent baselines, and extensive ablations covering augmentation count, architectures, dataset sizes, and computational cost

Strong results on benchmark tasks: Substantial improvements on worst-group accuracy (e.g., 66.1% vs 54.0% for ActGen on CelebA) with analysis showing ConfiG generates more challenging samples (Table 2)

Thorough ablation studies: Systematic investigation of design choices, complementarity with existing methods (TAB), and cost-quality tradeoffs demonstrating 2× ConfiG outperforms 10× baseline augmentations
Theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 provides formal justification connecting augmentation design to generalization error reduction with complete proofs in appendix
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core contribution is a straightforward combination of existing techniques (guided diffusion, knowledge distillation, confidence-based guidance). Equation 7 simply maximizes teacher confidence and minimizes student confidence—incremental over ActGen's similar student-aware generation

Severe practical limitations undermine applicability: Requires a robust teacher generalizing to unseen groups, creating a fundamental contradiction (if such a teacher exists, why use distillation at all?). For SpuCo Birds, authors could not use intended CLIP teacher and had to fine-tune on balanced data 'which would not be possible in practice.' Student performance on CelebA 'arguably limited by the CLIP teacher.' Hope that foundation models will cover all test distributions is optimistic but unverified

Substantial computational overhead: 11.4 sec/image (vs 2.1 sec for Stable Diffusion, 3.3 sec for ActGen), requiring 5 optimization steps with per-step decoding. Only generates 2× augmentations due to cost. Cost analysis relegated to appendix despite being a critical practical limitation

Theoretical analysis with strong assumptions providing limited actionable insights: Proposition 1 requires difficult-to-verify bounds (||t(x)−p*(x)||∞ ≤ δt, ||f(x)−t(x)||∞ ≤ δs) and restrictive condition δt+δs < 1/L. Gap between theory (cross-entropy loss) and practice (KL divergence). Bound involves multiple parameters difficult to control independently. Doesn't explain mechanism for why disagreement targets spurious vs hard features

Artificial experimental setup limits generalizability: Hyperparameter tuning only on groups present in training data doesn't reflect realistic deployment. Extremely limited datasets (500 images, 250 per class) unrepresentative of real scenarios. Completely missing groups is artificial covariate shift. Improvements diminish with scale—Table 7 with 1500 images shows smaller gains (7% vs 13% on worst-group)

Mixed performance on realistic settings: ImageNet results show ConfiG as second-best for validation accuracy with marginal improvements. Weaker performance when training sets are larger, suggesting method's benefits are primarily on small, curated benchmarks

Incomplete technical justification: Design choice γ=2 in Eq. 7 only empirically justified ('we find γ=2 to perform well') without systematic ablation. Limited analysis of why ConfiG improves over ActGen beyond loss formulation differences. No failure case analysis or discussion of when method might not work

Scope limitations: Only addresses group shift and class-specific spurious features. Limited engagement with domain adaptation, group robustness, and fairness literature. No comparison with methods from these related areas

Presentation issues: Important limitations (strong teacher requirement) buried in conclusion. Key results scattered across appendices. Dense notation in Section 3.1. Figure 2 analysis (teacher-student agreement) only on CelebA. Missing investigation of which spurious features are being targeted

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned. Method requires careful tuning (null-text inversion prompts, optimization steps, learning rates). Auxiliary student training effectiveness not thoroughly validated

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing knowledge distillation under covariate shift with unknown spurious features, with clear practical relevance
Novel confidence-guided approach leveraging teacher-student disagreement to generate targeted augmentations that are intuitive and well-justified
Theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) providing formal justification for the approach, with clear decomposition of generalization error

Strong and consistent empirical improvements across three datasets: CelebA worst group 54.0→66.1%, SpuCo Birds 52.7→62.7%, with comprehensive ablations on architectures, dataset sizes, and augmentation ratios
Thorough experimental evaluation including quantitative (Table 2) and qualitative analysis (Figures 3-4) validating that ConfiG targets spurious features and generates more challenging samples
Interesting discovery of unknown spurious correlations (eye color in CelebA) demonstrating robustness of the approach
Clear presentation with well-structured motivation, methodology, and extensive appendices facilitating reproducibility
Careful experimental design with fair baseline comparisons and multiple evaluation metrics (worst-group, group-mean, sample-mean accuracy)
weaknesses: Critical practical limitation: requires a robust teacher accurate on both training and test distributions; SpuCo Birds example shows CLIP achieved only 40.2% worst-group accuracy, necessitating fine-tuning on balanced data, contradicting the foundation-model motivation
Substantial computational overhead: 11.4 sec/image vs 2.1-3.3 sec for baselines (5-5.5× slower), with unclear practical tradeoffs even when quality-vs-quantity argument is considered

Loose theoretical bounds: Proposition 1 relies on multiple small-error assumptions (δ_t, δ_s, δ_t + δ_s < 1/L) that are difficult to verify in practice; the condition on Θ and α are abstract and provide weak quantitative guidance

Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (guided diffusion + teacher-student disagreement) without fundamental algorithmic innovation; design choices (γ=2, 5 optimization steps, 0.01 learning rate) lack thorough ablation

Experimental setup concerns: spurious features artificially introduced via subsampling rather than naturally occurring; only binary/coarse classification tasks (CelebA, SpuCo Birds binary; ImageNet 100 classes); unclear generalization to subtle, high-dimensional spurious features
Performance gap on Spurious ImageNet: ConfiG achieves 81.5% mAUC (second-best), with DAFusion at 80.3%, showing less convincing improvements on this dataset
Incomplete baseline comparisons: limited engagement with robustness-without-demographics and group robustness literature beyond TAB ablation; no comparison with domain adaptation methods
Statistical concerns: overlapping error bars in some results (Table 1), only 3 runs per experiment without significance testing or p-values

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and formalizes the challenge of knowledge distillation under covariate shift with limited training data coverage
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets with group labels, multiple metrics (SMA/GMA/WGA), extensive ablation studies, and comparison with 7+ baselines
Thorough documentation: Extensive appendices with hyperparameters, failure analysis, computational costs, and additional experiments
Theoretical foundation: Provides formal analysis (Proposition 1) attempting to justify the approach, though with limitations
Effective visualization: Figures clearly illustrate the covariate shift problem and demonstrate how the method generates challenging samples
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core contribution is combining existing techniques (diffusion-based augmentation + confidence guidance + inter-class mixing). Confidence-guided generation and these augmentation components are not novel individually

Modest empirical improvements with high computational cost: Many improvements are within standard deviations (e.g., CelebA-HQ: 97.76% vs 97.75% for ActGen), while Table 11 shows ConfFQ requires 2.8×10¹¹ FLOPs—approximately 2-3x more than simpler baselines like GIF. Cost-effectiveness is inadequately addressed

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Proposition 1 relies on strong, unvalidated assumptions (Eqs. 13-15). The assumption of a teacher that 'approximates p* well' is restrictive. The gap between theory and empirical results is not well explained

Experimental scope limitations: Only evaluated on image classification with synthetic group-based covariate shifts (gender, age, bird backgrounds). Unclear if improvements hold under natural distribution shifts or without explicit group labels. No evaluation on detection, segmentation, or other modalities

Insufficient ablation and mechanistic understanding: Why does inter-class mixing help? Why is confidence guidance superior to pure disagreement maximization? What characteristics make the augmentations effective? Failure case analysis (Appendix O) is superficial

Fairness of comparisons: While attempting to address computational budget matching, comparisons are still not straightforward—different methods use different augmentation counts, and some baselines may use suboptimal hyperparameters

Method requires restrictive assumptions: Demands a well-calibrated teacher model approximating the true distribution, access to group labels during evaluation, and specific types of covariate shift. Limited applicability in practice

Missing key analyses: No cost-accuracy trade-off study, no comparison with simple baselines (augmentation + rebalancing), no wall-clock time analysis, unclear benefits vs. collecting more real data on underrepresented groups

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing knowledge distillation under covariate shift with clear practical relevance and intuitive problem formulation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets with multiple metrics (SMA, GMA, WGA), extensive ablations, and 7 strong baselines with reported standard deviations
Consistent and substantial improvements in worst-group accuracy (e.g., SpuCo Birds: 45→73%, BAR: 59→69%), addressing the most challenging robustness metric
Principled methodology combining inter-class mixing, latent optimization, and confidence-guided diffusion with theoretical motivation via Proposition 1
Thorough documentation including hyperparameters, training details, computational cost analysis, and supplementary experiments with different teacher/student configurations
Honest discussion of limitations and scope, acknowledging that method requires pre-trained teachers and applies to classification tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - individual components (diffusion augmentation, soft-target distillation, inter-class mixing) are well-established; main contribution is their combination rather than new fundamental techniques

Theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions (Eqs. 13-15) including bounded KL divergence; bounds are loose and provide motivation rather than rigorous guarantees, with no finite-sample complexity analysis
Significant computational overhead of ~8× relative to baseline augmentation methods (Table 11), limiting practical applicability in resource-constrained settings

Narrow evaluation scope limited to image classification with demographic/background covariate shifts; no evaluation on other domains, shift types, or non-augmentation-based robust learning methods (e.g., DRO)
Insufficient analysis of failure modes (Section O provides only 2 categories); limited investigation of out-of-distribution augmentations or systematic characterization of failure conditions
Reliance on well-trained teacher models; Table 7 shows weaker teachers diminish ConfG's advantage, with limited guidance on teacher selection or handling of weak teachers

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed - only α is ablated (Tables 19-20), while guidance scale and diffusion steps lack sensitivity analysis; different α across datasets without principled selection criteria

Missing comparisons with recent group robustness methods beyond augmentation (e.g., DRO variants, fairness-aware training) and simpler baselines; comparisons limited primarily to diffusion-based methods
